oil.summary: Crude benchmarks posted a solid one-day recovery — WTI +1.75% to $76.56 and Brent +2.06% to $81.14 — but both remain sharply lower on the week (-8.4% and -8.9% respectively), underscoring the volatile backdrop. Gulf shipping ground to a near-halt after Houthis claimed to have struck a Saudi oil tanker, while three tankers were separately reported damaged amid the broader US-Iran conflict. Ukraine's long-range drone strike on one of Russia's largest refineries added a fresh supply-disruption bid. On the demand side, Sinopec is pivoting to Russian Far East crude for Q3, and Indian state refiners are aggressively buying West African barrels as Middle East supply uncertainty bites. A potential Iran-Oman deal on joint Hormuz management offered a partial offset to risk premium. RBOB gasoline was a glaring outlier, cratering 6.1% on the day and nearly 19% on the week — the data provides no direct headline explanation for that move.
drivers: Gulf tanker disruptions and Houthi strike claim on Saudi oil tanker reinforce near-term supply-risk premium in crude
Ukraine drone attack on a major Russian refinery adds further upstream and refining supply concern
RBOB gasoline collapsed 6.1% intraday and 18.8% on the week — no supporting headline provided; warrants close monitoring

gas.summary: The Henry Hub/TTF divergence widened sharply today: TTF surged 5.80% to 55.445 €/MWh while Henry Hub fell 2.46% to $2.621/MMBtu, now down 18.4% on the month. The TTF spike is directly tied to a headline that European gas storage has fallen to its lowest level since 2011, compounding a Middle East conflict that has disrupted LNG flows and thrown the LNG growth story into doubt. Belgium's July LNG imports were entirely sourced from Russia as alternative cargoes dried up — a sign of acute market stress. On a longer-horizon constructive note, Nigeria is targeting $30–50 billion across 22 offshore projects, Angola confirmed new reserves via the Katambi-2 appraisal well, and Argentina's Vaca Muerta shale output is setting production records, but none of these developments provide near-term relief for European winter supply.
drivers: European gas storage at lowest since 2011 drives TTF +5.8% as winter supply anxiety mounts
Middle East conflict severely curtails LNG availability into Europe, with Belgium forced to source 100% of July LNG from Russia
Henry Hub continues to slide (-2.5% today, -18.4% month) on ample North American supply, widening the transatlantic price dislocation

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up 0.75% to $77.60, building modestly on a month-to-date gain of 3.76%, supported by the same TTF spike (+5.8%) that is lifting European power generation costs. Europe's heatwave is delivering a double hit: refineries are losing cooling efficiency and river levels are forcing cuts to nuclear generation output, tightening the power balance at precisely the moment storage is most depleted. A drone strike on a UAE nuclear power plant was also flagged this week, adding a geopolitical dimension to nuclear supply risk. On the demand side, big tech's accelerating pivot to fuel cells for AI data centers represents an emerging structural shift in power procurement. China, meanwhile, supplied all net global nuclear power growth in 2025, underlining diverging capacity trajectories between East and West.
drivers: European heatwave impairing both refinery operations and nuclear output, tightening regional power supply and supporting EUA prices
TTF at 55.45 €/MWh (+5.8% today) raises gas-fired generation costs, adding upward pressure on wholesale power and carbon prices
Drone attack on UAE nuclear facility and lowest-since-2011 EU gas storage levels compound winter energy security concerns across the power complex
sources: Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs
